catalog_quote: [Stresemann 1927 p. 174] Das Ur-Ambon betonte alle mehr als einsilbigen Wörter auf der Pänultima des Grundwortes. Einsilbige Suffixe, welcher Art auch, übten auf die Lage des Tones keinen Einfluß aus. ... Das Asilulu, Hila und Haruku betonen infolgedessen noch immer wie das SA. auf der nunmehrigen Drittletzten, wenn das Grundwort durch einen Konsonanten geschlossen war, z. B.: Himmel As., Hi. lánit-e, Har. lánit-o | Mond As., Hi. húlan-e, Har. húran-o. Salz Har., Hi. tási'-e, As. sási'-e [p. 176] Das UA. Verbalsuffix -ke läßt im Asilulu, Hila, Nuaulu und Haruku den Ton noch unbeeinflußt. ... wünschen Har. pála-e ... Das Verbalsuffix -lo läßt den Ton im Haruku unbeeinflußt: „stützen" tóa-lo, „meißeln" hatéte-lo. [van Hoëvell 1877 p. 11] 't Verschil bestaat evenwel alleen in 't leggen van den klemtoon. Terwijl de christen-inlander op Harœkœ den algemeenen regel volgt om 't accent te leggen op de voorlaatste lettergreep, laat de Mohamedaan den klemtoon gedurig verspringen. [pp. 13-14] Omtrent den klemtoon is op te merken, dat deze, evenals zulks in 't Maleisch veelvuldig het geval is, in den regel valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. In de dialecten van Harœkœ en Asilœlœ evenwel verspringt de klemtoon meermalen, en dikwijls op zeer grillige wijze. — Waar dit het geval is zal het teeken (') boven de lettergreep aanduiden, dat daarop de klemtoon vallen moet.

new_statements.translation: [p. 174] Proto-Ambon stressed all words of more than one syllable on the penult of the base word. Monosyllabic suffixes, of whatever kind, had no influence on the position of the stress. [...] Asilulu, Hila and Haruku consequently still stress, like Sub-Ambon, what is now the antepenult when the base word was closed by a consonant, e.g. 'sky' As., Hi. lánit-e, Har. lánit-o | 'moon' As., Hi. húlan-e, Har. húran-o. [p. 176] The Proto-Ambon verbal suffix -ke leaves the stress unaffected in Asilulu, Hila, Nuaulu and Haruku [...] 'wish' Har. pála-e [...] The verbal suffix -lo leaves the stress unaffected in Haruku: 'prop up' tóa-lo, 'chisel' hatéte-lo.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the base (root) word and stays there when the support vowel -o/-e, the verbal suffix -ke > -e, or the suffix -lo is added; so bare disyllabic roots are penult-stressed and suffixed words are stressed on the antepenult (lánit-o 'sky', húran-o 'moon', pála-e 'wish', hatéte-lo 'chisel'). Van Hoëvell 1877, whose Pelauw word list is the data behind this, states the same facts pre-analytically: the general rule is penultimate stress (as in Malay), but in the Haruku (Muslim-village) and Asilulu dialects the stress 'shifts frequently, often very capriciously', so he marks it with an acute wherever it is not penultimate; the stressed vowel is as a rule long.
new_statements.exceptions: Van Hoëvell 1877 p. 11: the Christian villages of Haruku (variety now extinct) followed the general penultimate rule, whereas the Muslim villages Pelauw, Kailolo, Kabauw and Rohomoni 'let the stress shift continually'; p. 12: article-suffixed nouns differ across dialects 'met gewijzigden klemtoon' (Sap. hulánno, Har. húrano, Asil./Hil. húlane 'moon'). Stresemann 1927 p. 176 contrasts Saparua/Nusalaut, where -e and -lo do shift the accent to the new penult (palá-e, tomá-lo). Neither source gives a lexical list of exceptions; van Hoëvell's 'grillige wijze' (capricious) suggests he could not state the morphological rule that Stresemann later extracted.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a word list (van Hoëvell's Pelauw list; Stresemann's comparative examples). Van Hoëvell 1877 verbatim: p. 11 'Het derde is het dialect van het eiland Harœkœ, waarbij echter valt op te merken, dat het in de slamsche [sic] negorijen Pelaœ, Kailolo, Kabaœ en Rohomoni nog eenigzins anders gesproken wordt dan in de christen-negorijen van datzelfde eiland. 't Verschil bestaat evenwel alleen in 't leggen van den klemtoon. Terwijl de christen-inlander op Harœkœ den algemeenen regel volgt om 't accent te leggen op de voorlaatste lettergreep, laat de Mohamedaan den klemtoon gedurig verspringen.' pp. 13-14 'Omtrent den klemtoon is op te merken, dat deze, evenals zulks in 't Maleisch veelvuldig het geval is, in den regel valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. In de dialecten van Harœkœ en Asilœlœ evenwel verspringt de klemtoon meermalen, en dikwijls op zeer grillige wijze. — Waar dit het geval is zal het teeken (') boven de lettergreep aanduiden, dat daarop de klemtoon vallen moet. — Nog zij aangeteekend, dat de vocaal in de lettergreep, waarop de klemtoon valt, in den regel lang moet worden uitgesproken.' Grimes & Edwards 2026 reprint the accented Haruku forms (hálat-o, húran-o, úran-o, wóru-i, mákel-o, sánaele) consistent with root-penult stress. Caveats: both sources are 19th/early-20th-century, rest on a single 1870s word list of the Pelauw dialect, and no modern instrumental or phonemic description confirms the rule; Stresemann's source kind is comparative-historical though the Haruku statements are synchronic.
new_statements.identity_note: Both statements concern the speech of the Muslim north-coast villages of Haruku (van Hoëvell 1877 p.11: 'Pelaoe, Kailolo, Kabaoe en Rohomoni'; his word list is explicitly the Pelauw dialect), which is what survives today as Haruku [hrk] haru1244 (Collins 1983 n.5: spoken in Kailolo, Kabau, Rohomoni, Pelau, Kariu, Hualiu, 'elsewhere on Haruku it is apparently extinct'; Grimes & Edwards 2026 give Kailolo the separate Glottolog dialect code kail1252 and cite van Hoëvell 1877 + Stokhof 1982a as the Haruku [haru1244] data sources). Van Hoëvell contrasts this with the Christian villages of the island, which in 1877 followed regular penultimate stress; that variety is now extinct. Stresemann 1927 did no Haruku fieldwork: his 'Har.' forms (lánit-o, húran-o, pála-e, tóa-lo, hatéte-lo) are van Hoëvell's accented Pelauw forms, so his rule is an analysis of the 1877 data. Poedjimah 1964 (Glottolog's only descriptive item) is on Pelau(w) too.

sources.note: Nothing for Haruku. Haruku appears as Kailolo field data (1978) and van Hoëvell/van Ekris lists in reflex tables; n.5: Haruku spoken in Kailolo, Kabau, Rohomoni, Pelau, Kariu, Hualiu, 'elsewhere on Haruku it is apparently extinct'.
